text: After this you can place engineering work within the wider system life cycle.

Technical work spans need analysis, requirements, architecture, design, implementation, verification, validation, transition, service and retirement. These activities overlap rather than occur once. Supplier agreements, management decisions and organizational resources support each stage. Separate plans for risks, information, cost, quality and configuration coordinate these connections.

items: Select the current service stage and the next decision. You should see: A clear decision to prepare. If not: Ask what must be agreed before technical work proceeds.
Identify the technical and management activities needed now. You should see: A short list of owners and evidence. If not: Include suppliers, users and support teams.
Check interfaces with the next life-cycle stage. You should see: Actions for transition, support or withdrawal. If not: Revisit the requirement and the operating environment.
Inferred: A new control system needs design evidence and an ongoing maintenance process before it enters service.

text: A calendar alone does not prove the work is ready.

items: Treating verification as a final event. Earlier defects remain hidden longer. Fix: Plan the evidence throughout development.
